title: Ask HN: Has AI coding changed who builds your internal tools?
summary:
In a large company, a dedicated team might build an internal tool that dozens of other teams use. If your team needs a feature for its own workflow, you have to explain the use case, agree on how it fits into the shared tool, and wait for it to get prioritised.

With AI coding tools, it might now be faster for the team that needs the feature to build and maintain its own tool or completely scratch the tool and rebuild it if need. I’m curious how that plays out once the tool has been in use for a while.

So is paradigm shifting where we remove centralisation of building internal tools and let teams decide?

title: Ask HN: What do you all use to share context with team mates?
summary:
Problem: My cofounder and I work exclusively in Claude code. However, I've no idea about the conversation he is having with his agents. The only point of contact is what gets merged in Github, which is the contract. But there are times when it would be very useful for me to understand the decisions/conversation that led him to arrive at this juncture. All this context is lost.

The current best methods I've found are 1. Team/Org/Dept level shared-context.md in a cloud folder - who updates?, when?, how often?, what level of summarization?, are all unknown 2. External Tools to store context - pg, supabase, any vectordb, but then you have to maintain it, and all the same questions apply 3. Use git to share context

I've not found a single satisfactory way to achieve this. We both have multiple Claude code sessions open right now and we have no good way to communicate what each of us is trying to achieve in the session.

title: Tell HN: Hardware flaws to confidential AI are probably worse than they let on
summary:
By "they", I mean services that advertise private AI inference running in confidential computing environments like Intel SGX/TDX.

My point is: I've seen arguments that RAM interposition showcased in tee.fail would probably be too obvious in a reputable data center, but you can seemingly just extract a key through a physical attack once and pretend to be that CPU in software thereafter.[1]

I'm not very knowledgeable in this topic, but how are users of this service meant to verify that the TDX verifications quotes aren't forged from a key extracted from a processor as seen in tee.fail?

[1] https://tee.fail/#:~:text=Recovering%20Attestation%20Keys%20from%20Intel%20Machines

title: I'm genuinely disappointed in our most visible tech leadership
summary:
Elon Musk, Jensen Huang, Alex Karp, Jeff Bezos, Bill Gates, etc, etc. I know the reasons why this stuff happens. Power is absolutely toxic to ethics, consequences are often minimal until a line is crossed, crossing the line is often not an immediate trigger to consequences, success breeds overconfidence, money breeds echo chambers of sychophantic feedback which trigger garbage-in-garbage-out decision making. That last one has always been a special trap for the rich and famous, killing them and their reputation with tremendous efficiency for most of human history; but we're all kings of little AI domains now and can all curate our feedback to whatever feels best, ignoring any discomfort until it goes away.

Still. Knowing why it's happening doesn't stop the disappointment. Isn't anyone at that level aware of the GIGO problem? Does awareness make you less successful because responsible, prosocial, ordinarily intelligent actions are not profitable? What would be effective strategies to keep people at that level off drugs and relatively sane?
